{{short description|Injective polynomial functions are bijective}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
In mathematics, the '''Ax–Grothendieck theorem''' is a result about [[injectivity]] and [[surjectivity]] of [[polynomial]]s that was proved independently by [[James Ax]] and [[Alexander Grothendieck]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ax|first=James|authorlink=James Ax|title=The elementary theory of finite fields|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=Second Series|volume=88|year=1968|pages=239–271|doi=10.2307/1970573|issue=2|jstor=1970573}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Grothendieck|first=A.|authorlink=Alexander Grothendieck|title=[[Éléments de géométrie algébrique]]. IV. Étude locale des schémas et des morphismes de schémas. III. |pages= 103–104, Theorem 10.4.11|series=Inst. Hautes Études Sci. Publ. Math.|volume=28|year=1966}}</ref><ref name="Terence Tao">{{cite web |url= http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2009/03/07/infinite-fields-finite-fields-and-the-ax-grothendieck-theorem/#more-1869|title=Infinite fields, finite fields, and the Ax-Grothendieck theorem |accessdate= 2009-03-08|author=[[Terence Tao|Tao, Terence]] |date=2009-03-07|work=What's New| archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20090311031630/http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2009/03/07/infinite-fields-finite-fields-and-the-ax-grothendieck-theorem/| archivedate= 11 March 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref><ref name="Serre">{{cite book | last1=Serre | first1=Jean-Pierre | author1-link=Jean-Pierre Serre | title=Arithmetic, geometry, cryptography and coding theory | arxiv=0903.0517 | publisher=Amer. Math. Soc. | location=Providence, R.I. | series=Contemp. Math. | mr=2555994 | year=2009 | volume=487 | chapter=How to use finite fields for problems concerning infinite fields | pages=183–193| bibcode=2009arXiv0903.0517S }}</ref>

The theorem is often given as this special case: If <math>P</math> is an [[injective]] polynomial function from an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[complex vector space]] to itself then <math>P</math> is [[bijective]]. That is, if <math>P</math> always maps distinct arguments to distinct values, then the values of <math>P</math> cover all of <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math>.<ref name="Terence Tao"/><ref name="Serre"/>

The full theorem generalizes to [[Morphism of algebraic varieties|regular maps]] on any [[algebraic variety]] over an [[algebraically closed field]].<ref>[[Éléments de géométrie algébrique]], IV<sub>3</sub>, Proposition 10.4.11.</ref>

==Proof via finite fields==
Grothendieck's proof of the theorem<ref name="Terence Tao"/><ref name="Serre"/> is based on proving the analogous theorem for [[finite field]]s and their [[algebraic closure]]s. That is, for any field <math>F</math> that is itself finite or that is the closure of a finite field, if a polynomial <math>P</math> from <math>F^n</math> to itself is injective then it is bijective.

If <math>F</math> is a finite field, then <math>F^n</math> is finite. In this case the theorem is true for trivial reasons having nothing to do with the representation of the function as a polynomial: any injection of a finite set to itself is a bijection. When <math>F</math> is the algebraic closure of a finite field, the result follows from [[Hilbert's Nullstellensatz]]. The Ax–Grothendieck theorem for complex numbers can therefore be proven by showing that a counterexample over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> would translate into a counterexample in some algebraic extension of a finite field.

This method of proof is noteworthy in that it is an example of the idea that finitistic algebraic relations in fields of [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] 0 translate into algebraic relations over finite fields with large characteristic.<ref name="Terence Tao"/> Thus, one can use the arithmetic of finite fields to prove a statement about <math>\mathbb{C}</math> even though there is no [[homomorphism]] from any finite field to <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. The proof thus uses [[Model theory|model-theoretic principles]] such as the [[compactness theorem]] to prove an elementary statement about polynomials. The proof for the general case uses a similar method.

==Other proofs==
There are other proofs of the theorem. [[Armand Borel]] gave a proof using topology.<ref name="Serre"/> The case of <math>n=1</math> and field <math>\mathbb{C}</math> follows since <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is algebraically closed and can also be thought of as a special case of the result that for any [[analytic function]] <math>f</math> on <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, injectivity of <math>f</math> implies surjectivity of <math>f</math>. This is a corollary of [[Picard theorem|Picard's theorem]].

==Related results==
The inverse of <math>f</math> is always also a polynomial function in the case of complex numbers, i.e., <math>f</math> is an [[isomorphism of varieties]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rudin |first=Walter |author-link=Walter Rudin |date=1995 |title=Injective polynomial maps are automorphisms. |journal=Amer. Math. Monthly |volume=102 |issue=6 |pages=540–543 |mr=1336641}}</ref> More generally, a bijective morphism <math>f\colon Y\to X</math> of complex varieties is an isomorphism if <math>X</math> is [[normal variety|normal]], which can be deduced from [[Zariski's main theorem]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Inverse of a polynomial map |url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/232562/inverse-of-a-polynomial-map#232992 |access-date=2026-08-02 |website=MathOverflow |language=en}}</ref>

Another example of reducing theorems about [[morphism of finite type|morphisms of finite type]] to finite fields can be found in [[Éléments de géométrie algébrique|EGA IV]]: There, it is proved that a [[radicial morphism|radicial]] <math>S</math>-endomorphism of a scheme <math>X</math> of finite type over <math>S</math> is bijective (10.4.11), and that if <math>X/S</math> is of finite presentation, and the endomorphism is a monomorphism, then it is an automorphism (17.9.6). Therefore, a scheme of finite presentation over a base <math>S</math> is a cohopfian object in the category of <math>S</math>-schemes.

The Ax–Grothendieck theorem may also be used to prove the [[Garden of Eden (cellular automaton)|Garden of Eden theorem]], a result that like the Ax–Grothendieck theorem relates injectivity with surjectivity but in [[cellular automaton|cellular automata]] rather than in algebraic fields. Although direct proofs of this theorem are known, the proof via the Ax–Grothendieck theorem extends more broadly, to automata acting on [[amenable group]]s.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Ceccherini-Silberstein | first1 = Tullio
 | last2 = Coornaert | first2 = Michel
 | arxiv = 1011.4759
 | doi = 10.1112/jlms/jdr016
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Journal of the London Mathematical Society
 | mr = 2855789
 | pages = 541–558
 | series = Second Series
 | title = On algebraic cellular automata
 | volume = 84
 | year = 2011}}</ref>

Some partial converses to the Ax-Grothendieck Theorem:

*A generically surjective polynomial map of <math>n</math>-dimensional affine space over a finitely generated extension of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> or <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}[t]</math> is bijective with a polynomial inverse rational over the same ring (and therefore bijective on affine space of the algebraic closure).
*A generically surjective rational map of <math>n</math>-dimensional affine space over a Hilbertian field is generically bijective with a rational inverse defined over the same field. ("Hilbertian field" being defined here as a field for which Hilbert's Irreducibility Theorem holds, such as the rational numbers and function fields.)<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = McKenna | first1 = Ken
 | last2 = van den Dries | first2 = Lou
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02568417
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Manuscripta Mathematica
 | mr = 1037991
 | pages = 1–15
 | title = Surjective polynomial maps, and a remark on the Jacobian problem
 | volume = 67
 | year = 1990}}</ref>
